title: The Letter to the Hebrews
lead: An anonymous sermon with a letter's ending ('a word of exhortation', Hebrews 13:22), written in Greek that Origen already judged purer than Paul's, to a Christian community under pressure. It argues from the Greek Old Testament that Jesus, the Son, is better than the angels, Moses and the Levitical priests: a high priest forever after the pattern of Melchizedek, who offered himself once for all. Its warnings against falling away and its roll call of faith have shaped Christian teaching and debate ever since.

sections.h: What kind of writing it is
sections.b: Hebrews calls itself 'this word of exhortation' (13:22), the phrase Acts uses for a sermon in the synagogue (Acts 13:15). It reads like a sermon written down: it alternates teaching drawn from the Old Testament with warnings and appeals ('So...', 'Let us...'), and ends with a letter's greetings (13:22-25). It names neither its writer nor, outside the later title, its readers.

No one knows. The Greek East received it as Paul's from early on (Clement of Alexandria; Origen, who thought the wording another's and said 'who wrote the epistle, in truth, God knows'), while the Latin West long doubted. Barnabas, Luke, Clement of Rome, Apollos and Priscilla have all been proposed. See the authorship table on the book page.
